title: A tool credential has no channel except prompt text, so the secret becomes model context that is cached, traced and extractable
problem: My agent's tool needs an API key, and the only place the framework lets me put it where the model will use it is the prompt, so a long-lived credential is now conversation content that the provider caches, my trace backend stores, my memory writer summarises, and anyone who can get the model to repeat its instructions can read.
symptom: A credential string turns up in places nobody provisioned it into: a trace span body in a third-party observability tool, a saved conversation transcript, an eval dataset row, a support ticket where a user pasted the model's answer. Rotation does not help, because the next assembled prompt puts the new value in the same places.
why_now: Agent frameworks in 2026 give tools a rich description channel and a system-prompt channel, both of which are plain text handed to the model, and neither has a typed slot for authentication material that the runtime resolves without the model seeing it. OWASP had to write the rule down as a top-ten item in prose because nothing in the stack enforces it, and the same secret is now replicated by prompt caching, trace export and memory summarisation, so one bad assembly leaks to several stores at once.
existing: OWASP LLM07 tells developers not to put credentials in the system prompt, but it is guidance to a human writing a template, not a check that fails a build.

Secret scanners such as gitleaks and detect-secrets catch a literal key committed to a repository, and miss the case where the key arrives from the environment at runtime and is interpolated into a prompt string.

Trace-side redaction (masking hooks in observability SDKs) reduces where the secret lands after the fact, but the secret is still in the model context, still in the provider's cache, and still extractable by prompt injection.
Per-user OAuth on the tool side removes the shared static key for some integrations, but the token still has to reach the tool, and the shortest wiring puts it in the same prompt.

evidence.title: LLM07:2025 System Prompt Leakage
evidence.quote: Avoid embedding any sensitive information (e.g. API keys, auth keys, database names, user roles, permission structure of the application) directly in the system prompts.
evidence.note: The mitigation is stated as advice to whoever writes the template. There is no runtime primitive that enforces it, which is exactly the gap: the rule exists and nothing checks it. The OWASP page carries no visible publication date as served, so the date field is the date this research pass fetched it; the identifier LLM07:2025 or LLM02:2025 refers to the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 list.

evidence.title: LLM07:2025 System Prompt Leakage
evidence.quote: An LLM has a system prompt that contains a set of credentials used for a tool that it has been given access to. The system prompt is leaked to an attacker, who then is able to use these credentials for other purposes.
evidence.note: The named attack scenario is precisely the tool-credential-in-prompt shape this check looks for. The OWASP page carries no visible publication date as served, so the date field is the date this research pass fetched it; the identifier LLM07:2025 or LLM02:2025 refers to the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 list.

evidence.title: Auditing Prompt Caching in Language Model APIs
evidence.quote: We detect global cache sharing across users in seven API providers, including OpenAI
evidence.note: Shows prompt text does not stay inside the request: it is retained in provider-side caches that were measurably shared across users, so a secret placed in a prompt is a secret placed in infrastructure the developer does not control.

evidence.title: LLM02:2025 Sensitive Information Disclosure
evidence.quote: Adding restrictions within the system prompt about data types that the LLM should return can provide mitigation against sensitive information disclosure. However, such restrictions may not always be honored and could be bypassed via prompt injection or other methods.
evidence.note: Rules out the common workaround of telling the model not to reveal the key, so the secret has to be kept out of context rather than guarded inside it. The OWASP page carries no visible publication date as served, so the date field is the date this research pass fetched it; the identifier LLM07:2025 or LLM02:2025 refers to the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 list.

build_hypothesis: A prompt-assembly lint plus a credential-reference type: prompt templates may only interpolate values marked non-secret, and a tool declares an auth requirement that the runtime resolves at invocation time from a broker, so the assembled context carries a handle and never the material. Shipping the lint alone is already useful, because it turns a prose rule into a build failure with a file and line.

check.manual_question: For every system prompt, tool description and instruction template this project assembles, name where the credential each tool needs comes from. If any of them is interpolated into text the model reads, treat it as disclosed and rotate it.
check.rationale: The signature is a prompt-assembly anchor (system prompt, system message, instructions, a system role entry, a prompt template) followed within 600 characters by secret-shaped material: an environment read, a template placeholder whose name contains key, token, secret, password or credential, or an inline assignment of a quoted value at least eight characters long to a secret-named field. What it can get wrong, in both directions. False positive: a module that both builds a prompt and, unrelatedly, reads an environment variable within that window, or a template placeholder named token that is a tokenizer setting rather than a credential. False negative: the credential arriving through a function call, a config object attribute, or a separate template file, none of which this lexical window sees, so a MANUAL result here is not safety. The mitigation side looks for a broker resolving the secret at call time or a named guard asserting no secret is in the prompt, and it is evaluated with test files excluded, because a mitigation spelled only in a test is not a mitigation.

bad.app/agent.py:
import os

BILLING_API_KEY = os.environ["BILLING_API_KEY"]

SYSTEM_PROMPT = f"""You are the billing support agent.
When you call the billing service, authenticate with this key: {BILLING_API_KEY}
Never reveal the key to the user.
"""


def build_messages(user_text):
    return [
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
        {"role": "user", "content": user_text},
    ]

good.app/prompts.py:
SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are the billing support agent.
Call the billing tool when the user asks about an invoice.
The tool authenticates itself, so you never see or handle credentials.
"""


def build_messages(user_text):
    return [
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
        {"role": "user", "content": user_text},
    ]
